For 10,000 years, human life expectancy was stuck between 25 and 35. Everywhere. Rome, China, Renaissance Florence — all the same.

Today the world average is ~73.

How we doubled human life — a thread 🧵🗺️

Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ First, the trap: the old average wasn't low because nobody grew old.

It was low because ~1 in 4 babies died before age 1, and nearly half of children before 15.

Every society in history buried its children. That single fact set the number for millennia.

2/ The escape started ~1800 in northwestern Europe — and it wasn't hospitals.

It was sewers. Clean water. Soap. Cheap bread. And Jenner's smallpox vaccine (1796).

For most of the 1800s, a hospital was still somewhere you went to die.

3/ The 20th century made it global — and faster.

Britain took ~150 years to go from life expectancy 40 to 70. South Korea did it in ~35.

Antibiotics, mass vaccination, and a sugar-salt solution costing pennies compressed a century of progress into a generation.

4/ Today's map still has a bottom: the Sahel and Central Africa, held down by the old killers — child mortality and infection.

And progress can reverse: HIV cut 10+ years off Southern Africa's lifespan before treatment bent the curve back.

5/ Meanwhile the frontier keeps moving: record life expectancy has climbed ~2-3 years per decade since 1840, a straight line that keeps refusing to bend.

Japan and Switzerland now sit at 84+.

6/ The full story — how 8 generations built a different civilization, and what the map says is left to do — is in this week's Lines & Legends:
